title: handshake-latency-cost-profiles-microburst-walkthrough
summary: Working notes and annotated walkthrough of a small-burst (microburst) benchmark that isolates session handshake costs from per-token generation costs. Focused on: TLS/socket setup, runtime model handshake (KV init), and short-session tail impact on cost-per-query. Includes text charts and immediate ops recommendations.
body:
Purpose
- Capture and communicate the overlooked component of short-query economics: session handshake (TLS + connection + runtime model handshake) for microburst-heavy workloads (concurrent short sessions, few tokens each).
- Provide actionable knobs for product (client SDKs), runtime (prewarming), and sales (pricing guidance for high-churn customers).

Experiment setup (quick):
- Models: open-medium-13b (float16) pinned; policy: core-region vs edge-region; quantized variant available but not used in handshake timing step.
- Hosts: core (n1-standard + A100), edge (n1-highmem + T4).
- Client mix: 1k synthetic sessions/min, session length distribution: 80% 1–6 tokens, 20% 7–32 tokens. Burst shape: 10s spike every 60s.
- Measurement focus: separate out component timings: DNS/TCP/TLS, TLS handshake, TCP warmup, transport serialization, runtime handshake (KV cache init / model context mapping), first-token generation.

Key raw observations (representative numbers)
- Network-level (avg over test): DNS+TCP 6ms, TLS handshake 18ms, transport serialization 2ms.
- Runtime handshake (cold session, no KV): 42ms median, 110ms p95, 220ms p99.
- First-token generation (model): 28ms median, 40ms p95, 78ms p99.
- Combined cold-session p50: ~96ms, p95: ~170ms, p99: ~360ms.

Edge vs core differences (same test, different infra)
- Edge: TLS slightly faster (regional proximity): TLS 12ms vs 18ms; runtime handshake slightly slower due to smaller GPU kernel warmups: median 56ms (edge) vs 42ms (core).
- Resulting cold-session p95: edge 190ms vs core 170ms.

Cost-per-query impact model (simplified)
- Assumptions: throughput capacity priced per-GPU-hour; amortized GPU cost: $10/hr/core, $6/hr/edge node equivalent. Token CPU/network overhead minimal for short sessions.
- If we can reduce handshake p95 from 170ms -> 70ms via prewarm/persistent sockets, the queries/hr per GPU increases by ~30% for this microburst mix (sessions being short dominates).
- Rough delta: cost-per-1k-queries drops from $X to $X*0.77 (operationalized in downstream pricing). (X placeholder left for finance attach; but relative delta stands).

ASCII charts (text form) 
- Session latency CDF snapshot (cold vs prewarm) - percentiles in ms
  header:  p50   p90   p95   p99
  cold:    96    180   170   360
  prewarm: 48    110   70    120

- Burst timeline (10s spike) - requests/sec and observed p95 latency (example excerpt)
  time(s):   0    2    4    6    8   10  12  14
  rps:        10   120  330  280  110  20  12  8
  p95-ms:     90   150  360  310  160  95  70  60

- Component stack breakdown (median) for a cold short session (single token output)
  1) DNS/TCP: 6ms
  2) TLS handshake: 18ms
  3) Transport/serialization: 2ms
  4) Runtime handshake (KV init): 42ms
  5) First-token gen: 28ms
  total: 96ms

Interpretation and pitfalls
- Short sessions amplify handshakes: when per-query generation is <100ms, connection and runtime handshake dominate. Many SLOs (p95 targets) appear to be model-limited but are actually network/runtime handshake limited.
- Edge nodes reduce network latency but sometimes increase runtime handshake due to lighter/less-optimal kernel pools causing slightly higher model-init jitter. Net effect varies by workload.
- TLS reuse + HTTP/2 or persistent sockets are high-impact for microburst workloads. For HTTP/1 short-lived connections, TLS handshake alone can be >15% of p95.
- Cache warming strategies (KV prefill, pinned session pools) reduce runtime handshake but increase cost standing (idle pinned slots). Need economic tradeoff model.

Ops recommendations (quick action items)
- Client SDK: enable persistent connections by default, provide explicit keepalive guidance and an opt-in lightweight session handshake API for very short sessions (recommendation TTL 60s).
- Runtime: add fast path for session handshake: lightweight KV skeleton for short sessions that omits full context mapping when session size < 8 tokens. Feature flag behind an experiment.
- Console: add a "handshake" breakdown visualization in per-route latency waterfall (token-level + session-level).
- Pricing/Commercial: define a SKU for "high-churn microburst" customers with recommended persistent socket enablement and discounted committed prewarmed slots.

Experiment ideas for follow-ups
- Measure impact of pre-warmed pinned sessions vs ephemeral with persistent sockets across real customer traffic (A/B).
- Run a sweep of runtime handshake improvements (KV lazy-init, skeleton context) and quantify p95 delta and cost per 1k queries.
- Compare HTTP/1.1 short-lived vs HTTP/2 multiplexed vs gRPC streams under identical burst patterns.

Open questions / risks
- How does multi-tenant isolation policy (slot allocation) interact with pinned session pools? Could pinned slots lead to noisy neighbor issues? Need SRE-run stress tests.
- Security posture: session-level reuse has implications for per-request identity and audit logs. Ensure we preserve token-level audit while reusing transport sessions.

Appendix - quick commands / artifacts
- Synthetic driver: github:repo/bench-scripts#microburst-driver (run with --session-distribution short)
- Confluence: OPT-1254 (design notes on handshake api)
- Jira: OPT-3721 (experiment to implement KV skeleton)

Notes to self (todo)
- Convert relative cost deltas to absolute $ with finance help (attach real GPU amortization).
- Add a small slide deck for sales explaining "why short queries cost more" with two customer-ready visuals.
- Run edge/core kernel pool tuning experiment and collect p99 jitter numbers.

-- end of draft --
